Prepared: 31 October 2026 · Application: svara-app 0.1.0 · Developer: SutraCore

This folder explains how to use, configure, install, and hand over the current application. Screenshots come from the running app at http://localhost:3000 using the supplied demonstration account. Provider reference screenshots show public documentation, not a configured customer account.

Open final-release.html for the complete illustrated guide in a browser. It works offline and embeds its screenshots. The individual Markdown documents below are the editable source.

Files supplied

This public documentation includes guides, screenshots, a logo, and a placeholder environment template. The executable helper scripts described below are supplied with the purchased application source package; commands that reference them are run from that application root.

  • screenshots/: original browser captures used in the documents.
  • config/.env.example: placeholder-only configuration; copy it to the application root as .env and fill in customer-owned credentials.
  • scripts/create-release.ps1: packages current source and docs into a ZIP, excluding dependencies, generated output, credentials, and local development files.
  • scripts/initialize-plans.sql: inserts the three default plan definitions into a new initialized database.
  • scripts/build-guide.cjs: rebuilds the HTML reader from these Markdown documents using the installed marked and sharp modules (node docs/scripts/build-guide.cjs from the app root).
  • scripts/verify-docs.cjs: checks local document links and screenshot references.

Release boundary

The source ZIP contains application code and documentation. PostgreSQL records, R2 uploads, external service accounts, Stripe subscriptions, and real credentials are separate assets. Copying the app folder does not copy those services. Give the customer access to their hosting, DNS, database, Cloudflare, Resend, and Stripe accounts through the providers' normal account-management tools.

The supplied test login is for this demonstration environment. It is not created automatically in a fresh database. The application currently displays demonstration credentials on its public authentication pages; remove that content and the test prefills before production delivery. See the launch notes in document 08.

The live review confirmed navigation and page contents. It did not send invitations or OTP emails, change passwords, register security keys, modify paid subscriptions, delete records, or deploy the application. Onboarding is described from source because this account has already completed it. Source findings and outstanding launch checks are explicitly identified throughout the guide.

01 — Authentication and first access

Code examples and source files ↓

Documentation index · Next: Workspaces

1. Sign in

Open http://localhost:3000/auth/signin. On a customer deployment, replace http://localhost:3000 with the deployed HTTPS address.

  1. Enter your Email Address and Password.
  2. Select Keep me signed in only on a device you trust.
  3. Select Sign in.
  4. An account that has completed onboarding opens /dashboard. A new account opens /auth/onboarding.

The supplied local demonstration account is test@test.com / 12345678. This is sample access only. A fresh installation requires a newly registered, verified customer account, or a separately restored database.

Google and GitHub buttons: the buttons exist, but lib/auth.ts does not configure socialProviders. These methods need developer configuration and provider credentials before they work. There are no Google/GitHub environment variables currently read by the app. Adding variables alone will not enable social sign-in.

Passkey sign-in: select Sign in with passkey only if a passkey has already been registered for this application and domain. Follow the browser/device prompt. See document 04 for registration.

2. Create an account

Select Sign up, or open /auth/signup.

  1. Enter a name of at least two characters.
  2. Enter an email address you can receive mail at.
  3. Select the correct country code and enter a valid mobile number. Email addresses and mobile numbers must be unique.
  4. Enter and confirm the password. The current form enforces at least eight characters; use a stronger unique password for customer accounts.
  5. Select Create account and continue to email verification.

Registration does not automatically sign you in. Email verification is required by the server. The mobile field is account information; this implementation does not provide SMS verification.

3. Verify email

Open /auth/verify-email if you are not already taken there.

  1. Confirm the email address.
  2. Copy the six-digit OTP from the verification email.
  3. Enter the OTP and select Verify email.
  4. After success, sign in with the verified address and password.

The configured OTP lifetime is five minutes. Select Resend OTP when a fresh code is needed. Check spam folders and ask the installer to inspect Resend delivery logs if no email arrives. Email credentials are configured on the server, as explained in document 06.

4. Recover a forgotten password

From sign-in, select Forgot password?.

  1. Enter the registered email address and select Send OTP.
  2. After receiving the email, select the Reset password link. The request page does not automatically complete the reset.
  3. On /auth/reset-password, enter the email, OTP, new password, and matching confirmation.
  4. Select Reset password and sign in again after the success message.

The Account settings panel's password-update button is currently disabled. Use this OTP recovery flow for a password reset. Do not give support personnel your OTP or new password.

5. Complete two-factor sign-in

For an account with two-factor authentication enabled, sign-in requires a second verification step at /auth/two-factor.

Enter the current six-digit code from your authenticator app and select Verify. If the authenticator is unavailable, select Use a backup code instead and enter an unused saved backup code. Two-factor setup is described in document 04. This screenshot shows the verification form only; the demonstration account's two-factor setting was not changed.

6. First-time onboarding

The implementation contains a three-step onboarding flow:

Step What to enter Result
Create your workspace A unique workspace name and optional logo The app derives a slug from the name
Choose your plan Free, Pro, or Enterprise Pro attempts a Stripe checkout; a selection alone does not prove payment
Almost there Optional business name and the required discovery-source answer Submits the workspace and marks onboarding completed

Screenshot coverage: the supplied account was already onboarded, so visiting /auth/onboarding redirects to the dashboard. No fresh account or onboarding screenshot was created. The workspace creation screenshot below shows the separately available settings form, which serves the same name/logo purpose; it is not the onboarding screen.

Current source issue: onboarding returns /billing/plan, including its Pro checkout return URLs. That route does not exist in this source; the plan selection route is /billing/plans. If onboarding completes but the next page is missing, open /dashboard or /billing manually. The developer should correct these URLs before a customer launch. Default plan records must also be seeded before a new workspace is created; see document 07.

7. Sign out and protected pages

Select your name/email at the bottom of the sidebar, then Sign out. This ends the current session. To review other sessions, use Setting → Session. Delete Account → Sign out all sessions signs out every device.

The server redirects unauthenticated requests for workspace pages to sign-in. / and /auth also redirect to sign-in, while /profile redirects to /setting. Signed-in, onboarded users who visit authentication pages are redirected back to the dashboard.

Implementation references: lib/auth.ts, lib/auth-client.ts, lib/validations/auth.ts, app/auth/, app/actions/onboarding.ts, and app/(workspace)/layout.tsx.

Code examples and source locations

The following are source excerpts for the developer. Preserve the surrounding validation, loading states, callbacks, and error handling when editing them. Passwords and OTPs come from the form; do not hardcode customer credentials.

Server authentication policy

In lib/auth.ts, emailAndPassword controls email verification and automatic sign-in. The emailOTP plugin controls OTP length/lifetime. Edit the existing configuration rather than creating a second auth instance.

ts
// lib/auth.ts — existing options inside betterAuth({...}).
emailAndPassword: {
  enabled: true,
  autoSignIn: false,
  requireEmailVerification: true,
},

// Existing plugin inside plugins: [...]. Keep its sender callback.
emailOTP({
  expiresIn: 60 * 5,
  otpLength: 6,
  sendVerificationOnSignUp: true,
  sendVerificationOTP: async ({ email, otp, type }) => {
    await sendAuthOtpEmail({ email, otp, type });
  },
}),

Password/name/mobile validation is defined in lib/validations/auth.ts; signup also validates on the server in app/auth/signup/actions.ts. Update both layers together when changing registration rules. Keep required verification in place for the customer release.

Sign-in and registration

ts
// app/auth/signin/page.tsx — request inside the existing form handler.
authClient.signIn.email(
  {
    email: values.email.toLowerCase(),
    password: values.password,
    rememberMe: values.rememberMe ?? true,
  },
  // Preserve the existing onSuccess/onError callbacks here.
);

// app/auth/signup/page.tsx — invokes server validation and account creation.
const result = await signUpWithValidationAction(values);

The sign-in default values read NEXT_PUBLIC_TEST_EMAIL and NEXT_PUBLIC_TEST_PASSWORD. Blank those public values for customer deployments and remove the separate demo card in app/auth/layout.tsx. Brand headings and form text are customized in the relevant page.tsx and app/auth/_components/auth-header.tsx; see document 09.

Verification and password recovery

These excerpts use the corresponding form's existing values variable. Each belongs in its own page handler.

ts
// app/auth/verify-email/page.tsx
authClient.emailOtp.verifyEmail({
  email: values.email.toLowerCase(),
  otp: values.otp,
});

// app/auth/forgot-password/page.tsx
authClient.emailOtp.sendVerificationOtp({
  email: values.email.toLowerCase(),
  type: "forget-password",
});

// app/auth/reset-password/page.tsx
authClient.emailOtp.resetPassword({
  email: values.email.toLowerCase(),
  otp: values.otp,
  password: values.password,
});

Two-factor sign-in, passkeys, and route protection

ts
// app/auth/two-factor/page.tsx — existing verification choices.
await authClient.twoFactor.verifyTotp({ code: code.trim() });
// The backup-code branch uses this alternative, not both calls together:
await authClient.twoFactor.verifyBackupCode({ code: code.trim() });

// app/auth/signin/page.tsx — existing passkey sign-in request.
const result = await authClient.signIn.passkey();

The server guard below is in app/(workspace)/layout.tsx. Keep page access checks on the server when changing navigation.

ts
const session = await auth.api.getSession({ headers: requestHeaders });
if (!session) {
  redirect("/auth/signin");
}

For the known onboarding URL correction, edit the existing successUrl, cancelUrl, and final redirectTo in app/actions/onboarding.ts to use a route that exists, such as /billing for the return and /billing/plans for plan selection. This is a recommended source change, not one applied by this guide.

02 — Workspaces and team access

Code examples and source files ↓

Documentation index · Previous: Authentication · Next: Dashboard

A workspace is the organization/team context used for members, subscriptions, and credits. Your personal profile and sign-in methods belong to your account. Always check the active workspace before viewing billing or inviting teammates.

1. Switch workspace

Select the workspace name at the top-left of the sidebar, then select an existing workspace. The name and slug at the top-left change to the selected workspace. Alternatively, open Setting → Workspace and select Set Active in the required row. The active row is labelled Active and its Set Active button is disabled.

The Create workspace menu item in the top-left dropdown has no action wired in the current source. Use the Create Workspace button in settings instead.

2. View workspace details

Open Setting → Workspace.

Column Meaning
Workspace Team/organization display name
Slug Unique identifier shown with a leading / in the interface
Status Active or inactive for your current session
Actions Set Active, Edit, and Delete

Two existing demo workspaces appear in the screenshots. Their presence does not mean that a fresh Free account may create two workspaces; new creations are checked against the current limits.

3. Create a workspace

  1. Select Create Workspace.
  2. Enter a unique Workspace name.
  3. Enter a unique Workspace slug, such as customer-studio. Use a simple lowercase identifier with hyphens.
  4. Optionally select Upload logo. Accepted files are PNG, JPEG, WebP, or SVG, up to 2 MB.
  5. Select Create Workspace and confirm that the new row appears. Use Set Active to choose it if needed.

Cloudflare R2 must be configured for image uploads. Creating a workspace initializes its Free allowance; buying Pro on one workspace does not automatically make every new workspace Pro. If you see a limit message, check the account's applicable plan before attempting another creation.

4. Edit a workspace

Select Edit in the workspace row, change the name, slug, or logo, then select Save Workspace. Editing selects that workspace as the active context in the current implementation. Confirm the selected workspace before continuing elsewhere. Names and slugs must not duplicate another workspace.

The backend uses Better Auth organization permissions for updates and deletion. If a member cannot save, ask the workspace owner or administrator to perform the operation. This guide does not promise that every visible button is available to every role.

5. Invite teammates

  1. Select the correct active workspace.
  2. Open Setting → Members.
  3. Enter the teammate's email and choose member, admin, or owner as appropriate. Grant ownership only to the intended workspace owner.
  4. Select Send invitation. Resend sends the invitation email.
  5. Review Team members and Pending invitations. Select Cancel beside a pending invitation when it should no longer be used.

The email link opens /auth/signin?invitationId=.... The recipient must sign in with the exact invited email. A new recipient should register, verify email, and then reopen the original invitation link to sign in. The sign-in flow accepts the invitation and redirects to the dashboard. If the workspace name does not update, select it from the workspace switcher: the custom join endpoint does not explicitly set the active organization.

Current limitations: this panel lists members but does not provide existing-member removal or role-edit controls. The custom join endpoint checks pending status and email match, but does not explicitly compare expiresAt; expiry enforcement and repeated-acceptance handling need developer review before launch. The legacy /auth/join page requires a real invitation ID and may accept an invitation as a side effect when opened while signed in; it was not opened for documentation capture.

6. Understand limits

These are the limits defined in lib/plans.ts at release time:

Plan Credits per workspace period Workspace creation limit Members per workspace
Free 10 1 3
Pro 100 5 25
Enterprise Unlimited in the current allowance model Unlimited Unlimited

Workspace creation is checked across the user's memberships using their best available plan. Member invitations use the selected workspace's plan. Credit usage and period information come from allowance records; confirm billing and allowance synchronization during acceptance testing.

Plan feature names such as sso, advanced_analytics, and api_key are entitlement identifiers. They do not establish that the corresponding customer feature screens have been implemented.

7. Delete a workspace

The Delete action removes a workspace through Better Auth. Treat it as a destructive operation. Confirm the intended workspace, arrange backups, and have the owner perform it deliberately. The application uses a browser confirmation prompt. Removing a workspace must not be assumed to cancel a Stripe subscription or clean up R2 files automatically; coordinate these separately.

Implementation references: app/(workspace)/workspace-actions.ts, app/(workspace)/workspace-shell.tsx, app/(workspace)/setting/workspace.tsx, app/(workspace)/setting/members.tsx, and app/api/invitation/join/route.ts.

Code examples and source locations

Workspace creation and allowance

app/(workspace)/workspace-actions.ts contains server actions for creation, update, deletion, switching, and invitations. This is an excerpt from createWorkspaceAction, after its authentication, limit, and uniqueness checks:

ts
const workspace = await auth.api.createOrganization({
  headers: requestHeaders,
  body: {
    name: normalizedName,
    slug: normalizedSlug,
    logo: input.logo,
  },
});

await initOrganizationAllowance(workspace.id);

Keep those checks and allowance initialization if changing workspace creation. UI fields and dialogs are in app/(workspace)/setting/workspace.tsx; first-time workspace creation is also handled by app/actions/onboarding.ts.

Switch and invite from the settings handlers

These excerpts use the existing handler variables in app/(workspace)/setting/settings-client-view.tsx:

ts
// Switch: the server action checks the organization through Better Auth.
const result = await setActiveWorkspaceAction(workspaceId);

// Invite: preserve the existing success/error handling and workspace checks.
const inviteResult = await inviteWorkspaceMemberAction({
  workspaceId: selectedWorkspaceId,
  email: inviteEmail.trim().toLowerCase(),
  role: inviteRole,
});

Workspace name/logo changes here are database-backed team settings. They do not replace the global Svara AI logo, favicon, brand name, or email branding. Document 09 explains that distinction.

Plan limits

Edit the matching entries in lib/plans.ts when the agreed customer limits change:

ts
// lib/plans.ts — current Free entry inside PLAN_LIMITS.
free: {
  credits: 10,
  maxWorkspaces: 1,
  maxMembers: 3,
  features: [],
  displayName: "Free",
  sortOrder: 0,
},

Update plan marketing text in both app/auth/onboarding/onboarding-flow.tsx and app/(workspace)/billing/plans/page.tsx. Plan definitions are also stored in plan_allowance; arrange a reviewed database update for existing installations. docs/scripts/initialize-plans.sql only inserts missing rows and does not overwrite an existing plan.

03 — Dashboard and navigation

Code examples and source files ↓

Documentation index · Previous: Workspaces · Next: Settings

Open /dashboard after signing in and completing onboarding.

1. Identify the navigation areas

Area How to use it
Workspace name, top-left Select an existing team workspace
Dashboard Return to the overview
Setting Open profile, workspace, members, sessions, and account-security panels
Billing View subscription information or the plan selection screen

The Docs navigation item inside the app is currently disabled. Open this docs folder or the offline HTML guide to read the release documentation.

2. Read the Overview

The current screen contains four cards: Total views, Recipients, Delivery rate, and Opened. Under them are acquisition distribution, a traffic-source table, and listener/completion/play metrics with a comparison chart.

These analytics are demonstration data. Values such as 254 views, 19 recipients, and 1,284 listeners are hardcoded in the source, not read from a live analytics service. The displayed update dates are sample text. Do not use these figures for customer reporting or business decisions.

The sidebar's plan/credit summary is loaded separately from database allowance records. It is not part of the hardcoded analytics. If it disagrees with Billing, use the reconciliation checks in document 08.

3. Filters and chart controls

The date-range dropdown offers Last 7 days, Last 4 weeks, and Last 3 months. The chart also has 1D, 5D, 1M, and 1Y controls. These update UI state, but the current sample dataset is not replaced with period-specific results.

Search, the notification icon, report/download actions, and menu entries such as Inspect, Duplicate view, and Save as default have no implemented analytics workflow in the current source. They should not be described as working exports, saved reports, or searchable live metrics.

4. Reach, Engagement, and Growth

Reach, Engagement, and Growth each show a placeholder panel. The screenshot shows Reach; the other two use the same placeholder implementation. These tabs do not yet provide additional analytics.

5. Disabled navigation

The following sidebar entries are marked disabled/coming soon in the source: Analytics, Comments, Episodes, Shows, Audio Editor, Noise Reduction, Voice Enhancer, Transcripts, Highlights, Docs, Keys, and Playground. No separate functional pages for these entries are included in this release.

A paid-plan feature list may mention capabilities whose screens are still placeholders or disabled. Confirm the contracted feature scope with the delivery team before presenting those capabilities to an end customer.

Implementation references: app/(workspace)/dashboard/page.tsx, app/(workspace)/dashboard-data.ts, app/(workspace)/workspace-shell.tsx, and lib/plans.ts.

04 — Settings panel, one section at a time

Code examples and source files ↓

Documentation index · Previous: Dashboard · Next: Stripe

Select Setting in the sidebar, or open /setting. All eight sections are tabs on this same route. Click the tab label; the current component does not read a ?tab=... URL parameter.

1. Profile

Use this panel to update your display name, mobile number, and profile image.

  1. Select Upload image to choose a PNG, JPEG, WebP, or SVG up to 2 MB.
  2. Edit Full name or Phone number as required.
  3. Select Save profile changes and check the success message.

Uploading an image places it in R2 first; saving the profile applies the returned URL to your account. The primary email is read-only and verification status is shown. The interface says email changes are managed by an administrator, but this repository does not supply an administrator email-edit screen. Contact the delivery team for an approved email-change process.

2. Workspace

Select Set Active to switch context. Use Create Workspace, Edit, Save Workspace, and Delete to manage workspace records as permitted by your role. See document 02 for dialog screenshots, field explanations, limits, and destructive-operation guidance.

3. Members

The top form sends invitations using an email address and role. Team members lists names, emails, roles, and joined dates. Pending invitations lists invitation email, role, expiry, and a cancellation control.

Choose the intended workspace first. Sending an invitation requires a configured Resend sender and sufficient workspace allowance. Existing-member role edits/removal are not available from this panel. Invitation acceptance limitations are documented in document 02.

4. Session

The table shows device/browser, IP address, creation time, expiry, and Revoke. The current session is labelled Current and cannot be revoked with its row button.

  • Revoke ends the selected other session.
  • Revoke other sessions ends every session except the current one.
  • To end your current session, use the account menu's Sign out.

Revoking a session can interrupt work on another device. The attached capture is cropped to the upper session rows so that other devices' public IP addresses are not included. Dates are demonstration-session metadata; customer exports should use appropriately redacted captures.

5. Account

This panel lists linked sign-in providers, their account identifiers, and when they were linked. The email/password method is Primary and marked Required. Non-primary providers can be unlinked when another method remains available.

Update password is disabled and marked coming soon. Entering values in its fields will not change the password. Use the sign-in page's Forgot password? flow instead. Social-provider buttons require additional server setup; they are not enabled by default.

6. Two-Factor

The panel shows whether two-factor authentication is enabled. The intended setup sequence is to enter the current password, select Enable two-factor authentication, add the displayed secret to an authenticator, save backup codes privately, and enter a six-digit code to verify setup. Subsequent sign-ins use the verification page documented in document 01.

Developer launch item: the current QR image URL sends the TOTP secret URI to api.qrserver.com for image generation. Replace this with local QR generation before directing production customers to use this setup flow. A TOTP secret and backup codes are credentials and must not appear in release screenshots or shared support messages. Setup was not performed during this documentation review.

If already enabled, disabling two-factor protection requires the current password and the deliberate Disable action. Preserve an alternative way to access your account before changing authentication methods.

7. Passkeys

Select Register new passkey, then follow the browser or device's biometric/security-key prompt. A registered passkey appears with its name and creation date. Use Sign in with passkey on the sign-in page afterward.

Passkeys need a compatible browser/device and a secure production origin. Localhost is suitable for development, but a passkey registered for localhost should not be expected to work on the customer domain. A row's Delete action removes that passkey; keep another working sign-in method before doing so. No passkey was added or removed for this guide.

8. Delete Account

This section contains two separate operations:

Action Effect
Sign out all sessions Revokes all of this account's sessions and sends the user back to sign-in
Delete account Requests permanent account deletion; the email confirmation must match, and the backend may require a password or recent authentication

Account deletion removes the account and related authentication records. Do not assume that it cancels subscriptions, deletes public uploads, or transfers workspace ownership. Arrange ownership, billing, data retention, and backups before using it. The deletion action was not executed during documentation capture.

Implementation references: app/(workspace)/setting/, especially settings-client-view.tsx, and app/(workspace)/workspace-actions.ts.

  workspaceId: selectedWorkspaceId,
  name: workspaceForm.name.trim(),
  slug: workspaceForm.slug.trim(),
  logo: workspaceForm.logo.trim() || undefined,
});

3. Members code

Edit the invitation form/table in app/(workspace)/setting/members.tsx. The existing invitation request is:

ts
const result = await inviteWorkspaceMemberAction({
  workspaceId: selectedWorkspaceId,
  email: inviteEmail.trim().toLowerCase(),
  role: inviteRole,
});

4. Session code

app/(workspace)/setting/session.tsx renders the session table. These are the two different existing handler requests; do not execute them together as a diagnostic:

ts
// One selected other session:
const result = await authClient.revokeSession({ token });

// The separate "Revoke other sessions" handler:
const othersResult = await authClient.revokeOtherSessions();

5. Account code

app/(workspace)/setting/account.tsx contains the linked-provider table and disabled password-update UI. The client view preserves at least one linked method:

ts
const canUnlinkAccounts = accounts.length > 1;

// Existing unlink handler request, after its guard:
const result = await authClient.unlinkAccount({
  accountId: account.accountId,
  providerId: account.providerId,
});

6. Two-Factor code

app/(workspace)/setting/two-factor.tsx renders setup/status. The shared client view handles setup and verification in separate handlers:

ts
// Setup handler:
const result = await authClient.twoFactor.enable({
  password: twoFactorPassword,
});

// Separate verification handler:
const verifyResult = await authClient.twoFactor.verifyTotp({
  code: verifyCode,
});

Before customer use, replace the external QR image implementation described earlier. Do not log or publish totpURI or backup codes while customizing this section.

7. Passkeys code

app/(workspace)/setting/passkey.tsx renders passkey rows. The separate register and list operations use the configured Better Auth client:

ts
// Register handler (starts a device/browser prompt):
const result = await authClient.passkey.addPasskey();

// Refresh the displayed list after a successful registration:
const listResult = await authClient.passkey.listUserPasskeys();

8. Delete Account code

app/(workspace)/setting/delete-account.tsx renders the danger panel. Its button enablement comes from the confirmation check below; it is not itself a server authorization check:

ts
const canDeleteAccount =
  confirmEmail.trim().toLowerCase() === user.email.toLowerCase();

The deletion handler and all-session revocation handler are in settings-client-view.tsx. Keep both deliberate actions, their error handling, and server-side access controls when changing the panel's wording or appearance.

05 — Stripe configuration and customer billing

Code examples and source files ↓

Documentation index · Previous: Settings · Next: Environment and services

Stripe configuration is an installer task. The dashboard's Billing screen does not provide API-key fields. Add the values to the server environment, then restart the application; rebuild when public URL variables change.

This is a reference capture from Stripe's API-key documentation, not a screenshot of the customer's Stripe account. Provider menus can change; use the linked official pages alongside these instructions.

1. Obtain the server key

Sign in to the customer's Stripe Dashboard. Select the intended sandbox/test environment first. Open API keys and obtain the server key for that environment. Store it as STRIPE_SECRET_KEY. A publishable pk_... key cannot replace a server key. The app accepts sk_... or rk_...; a restricted key needs permissions for all subscription, Checkout, customer, and portal operations used by this integration. Keep it on the server. See Stripe API keys.

2. Create a monthly Pro price

In Product catalog, add a Pro product and a recurring monthly price. The current app displays $29 for Pro, so either create the agreed matching price/currency or have the developer update the UI to match the actual Stripe price. Copy the price's price_... identifier into STRIPE_PRICE_PRO_MONTHLY_ID; a product's prod_... identifier is a different value. See Manage products and prices.

STRIPE_PRICE_ENTERPRISE_MONTHLY_ID is optional and registers an Enterprise plan in the Better Auth plugin when provided. The current customer plan page has a disabled Contact sales button, so it does not offer Enterprise self-service checkout. Free allowances are stored in the app's database and do not require a Stripe Free product or price.

The existing scripts/setup_stripe_plans.py can create products, prices, and entitlement features, but it is not required for manual setup. It creates new products/prices on each run, and its Enterprise price is $99/month while the UI says Custom. Have the billing owner review it before using it, especially against live credentials.

3. Configure the webhook

In Stripe Workbench → Webhooks, create an event destination for the deployed endpoint:

text
https://app.customer.example/api/auth/stripe/webhook

Select these events required by the Better Auth integration:

  • checkout.session.completed
  • customer.subscription.created
  • customer.subscription.updated
  • customer.subscription.deleted

Copy the endpoint's signing secret into STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET. It starts with whsec_ and is separate from the API key. For production, the URL must be reachable over HTTPS. See Stripe webhooks and the Better Auth Stripe setup.

For local testing, install/sign in to the official Stripe CLI and run this in a separate terminal:

powershell
stripe listen --forward-to localhost:3000/api/auth/stripe/webhook

Use the listener's printed signing secret in the local .env, then restart the local app. Keep the listener running while testing. The CLI listener secret and deployed endpoint secret are different. The endpoint is provided by app/api/auth/[...all]/route.ts; no extra app route needs creating.

4. Fill the environment

dotenv
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_test_replace_with_customer_test_key
STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_replace_with_endpoint_or_cli_secret
STRIPE_PRICE_PRO_MONTHLY_ID=price_replace_with_monthly_pro_price
STRIPE_PRICE_ENTERPRISE_MONTHLY_ID=
NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL=http://localhost:3000

The first three Stripe variables must all be present for the plugin to register. The billing action additionally checks their prefixes. NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL determines Checkout/portal return URLs; use the customer's HTTPS origin in production. The active billing flow is the Better Auth integration in lib/auth.ts and app/(workspace)/billing/actions.ts.

5. Configure the customer portal

In Stripe customer portal settings, save the intended branding, payment-method, invoice, and subscription/cancellation options. The app creates portal sessions through the API, so no public no-code portal link needs to be pasted into this app. Check which actions the billing owner wants customers to perform. See Configure the customer portal.

6. What the customer sees

Open Billing. A workspace without an active paid subscription is redirected to /billing/plans. Free is shown as the current option. Upgrade to Pro starts Stripe Checkout for the active workspace. Only proceed with payment during an agreed test or purchase.

A workspace with a recognized subscription sees Billing Overview, the plan label, renewal date, and Open billing portal. The current code treats active, trialing, and past_due subscriptions as recognized for this page, so its Active badge is not proof that all invoices are paid.

The supplied demo workspace shows an old renewal date and a Pro billing record while the allowance sidebar shows Free. These screenshots illustrate existing data; they are not evidence of a current paid invoice or a validated end-to-end billing setup.

7. Validate in test mode, then switch to live

Before live release, the billing owner/developer should complete an agreed sandbox checkout and confirm that webhook delivery succeeds, the subscription references the correct workspace, Billing updates, and the allowance becomes Pro with the expected credits. Test renewal and cancellation handling as well. Successful Checkout redirection alone is insufficient because allowance changes are driven by webhook callbacks in lib/auth.ts.

For go-live, obtain the live server key, live price IDs, and live endpoint signing secret. Replace all test values together and redeploy. Sandbox objects are separate from live objects, so test price IDs cannot be used with a live key. See Stripe environments and API keys.

No subscription, payment, portal setting, or Stripe resource was created or changed during this documentation task.

Code examples and source locations

Server key and plan registration

lib/auth.ts reads the server environment and registers Stripe only when its three required values are present:

ts
const stripeSecretKey = process.env.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY;
const stripeWebhookSecret = process.env.STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET;
const stripeProMonthlyPriceId = process.env.STRIPE_PRICE_PRO_MONTHLY_ID;

// Existing Pro entry inside the Stripe plugin's subscription.plans array:
{
  name: "pro",
  priceId: stripeProMonthlyPriceId,
},

The internal plan name pro must agree with lib/plans.ts and subscription upgrade requests. Changing a customer-facing label does not require renaming that internal identifier. Price amounts/currency live in Stripe; displayed plan cards live separately in app/(workspace)/billing/plans/page.tsx and app/auth/onboarding/onboarding-flow.tsx.

Checkout and webhook reference

This source excerpt from app/(workspace)/billing/actions.ts attaches Checkout to the authenticated active workspace. summary, requestHeaders, and getBaseAppUrl are defined by the surrounding action:

ts
const result = await auth.api.upgradeSubscription({
  headers: requestHeaders,
  body: {
    plan: "pro",
    referenceId: summary.activeOrganizationId,
    customerType: "organization",
    successUrl: `${getBaseAppUrl()}/billing`,
    cancelUrl: `${getBaseAppUrl()}/billing/plans`,
    disableRedirect: false,
  },
});

Keep the session/workspace checks before this request. The webhook is handled through the existing auth catch-all:

text
Stripe destination: /api/auth/stripe/webhook
Route entry point:  app/api/auth/[...all]/route.ts
Plugin and hooks:   lib/auth.ts
Allowance changes:  lib/plans.ts
Billing actions:   app/(workspace)/billing/actions.ts
Customer plan UI:  app/(workspace)/billing/plans/page.tsx

Edit the existing hooks when adjusting allowance synchronization; adding a second unauthenticated webhook implementation can result in inconsistent records or bypassed signature checks.

06 — Environment credentials, Cloudflare, and email

Code examples and source files ↓

Documentation index · Previous: Stripe · Next: Installation and ZIP

1. Locate and create .env

The local .env file belongs in the application root beside package.json, not inside app, public, or docs. Enable View → Show → File name extensions in Windows Explorer so the file does not accidentally become .env.txt.

From the extracted application folder:

powershell
Copy-Item -LiteralPath '.\docs\config\.env.example' -Destination '.\.env'

Use this command only when creating a new .env; open an existing file for editing instead of overwriting it. Fill in customer-owned values using a text editor or your hosting provider's environment-variable settings. Keep real credentials in the customer's secret store and transfer them separately from the source ZIP. Do not put server secrets in variables beginning with NEXT_PUBLIC_: those values can be included in browser code.

2. Database and authentication values

Variable Required for Where the value comes from
POSTGRES_USER Bundled Docker database Choose the database username before the first container initialization
POSTGRES_PASSWORD Bundled Docker database Generate a unique database password and save it privately
POSTGRES_DB Bundled Docker database Choose the database name, for example svara
POSTGRES_PORT Local Docker port mapping Choose an unused host port; default is 5432
DATABASE_URL App and Drizzle, always PostgreSQL provider's connection details, or the local Docker credentials above
BETTER_AUTH_SECRET Authentication Generate a random secret locally; it is not issued by Cloudflare or Stripe
BETTER_AUTH_URL Server auth base and email links Local origin or customer's deployed HTTPS origin
NEXT_PUBLIC_BETTER_AUTH_URL Browser auth client Same application origin
NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL Billing/onboarding return links Same application origin
NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL Canonical URLs, sitemap, social metadata Customer's public HTTPS origin; otherwise source defaults to a SutraCore domain
NEXT_PUBLIC_BASE_URL Legacy /auth/join server request Same origin when supporting this legacy page; invitation emails currently point to sign-in
NEXT_PUBLIC_TEST_EMAIL Optional demo form prefill Leave blank in production; never use a real private account as a public prefill
NEXT_PUBLIC_TEST_PASSWORD Optional demo form prefill Leave blank in production; this is public browser configuration, never a secret store

Generate the authentication secret locally:

powershell
node -e "console.log(require('node:crypto').randomBytes(32).toString('hex'))"

Paste the output into BETTER_AUTH_SECRET privately. Keep it stable across deployments and instances; a change can invalidate authentication state or make protected authentication data unusable. A database restore involving existing authentication data also needs the matching secret and an appropriate recovery plan.

Example local database URL:

dotenv
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://svara_user:URL_ENCODED_PASSWORD@localhost:5432/svara

URL-encode characters such as @, :, /, #, or % in the URL's password. A hosted database provider may supply SSL parameters; preserve its required connection/TLS settings. Inside an application container on the same Compose network, the database hostname would be postgres; this repository's Compose file starts only PostgreSQL, so the documented local app process uses localhost.

Changing POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env after a Docker data volume has been initialized does not itself change the password already stored in PostgreSQL. Use an explicit database credential-rotation procedure.

3. Cloudflare R2: create storage and credentials

This is a public documentation capture, not the customer's Cloudflare account.

  1. In the customer's Cloudflare account, enable R2 Object Storage and create a bucket for application images.
  2. Copy the account ID, not a website zone ID, into CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID.
  3. From R2 account details, open API-token management. Create a token with Object Read & Write restricted to this bucket.
  4. Save the returned S3 Access Key ID as R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID and Secret Access Key as R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY. Store the secret when it is displayed; it cannot be retrieved again later.

See Cloudflare R2 authentication.

Variable What to enter
CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID Account identifier used to build the R2 S3 endpoint
R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID R2 S3-compatible access key ID
R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY Matching S3 secret key, not a generic Cloudflare API token
R2_BUCKET Exact bucket name
R2_PUBLIC_URL Public image base URL, with https:// and no trailing slash
R2_PREFIX Optional folder prefix such as SvaraAI, without leading/trailing slashes

The app builds the default endpoint https://ACCOUNT_ID.r2.cloudflarestorage.com in lib/s3.ts. Jurisdiction-specific buckets need a matching endpoint code change; this version has no endpoint override variable.

4. Cloudflare R2: make application images accessible

Attach a customer-controlled custom domain such as assets.customer.example to the bucket and use https://assets.customer.example as R2_PUBLIC_URL. For development, an enabled r2.dev URL can be used. Cloudflare describes r2.dev as a development access method; use a custom domain for production. Public bucket contents are accessible to visitors who know the object URL. See Cloudflare public buckets.

The server writes images under a key like SvaraAI/workspace-logos/USER_ID/TIMESTAMP.png. Both profile pictures and workspace logos use this upload endpoint. The returned URL is R2_PUBLIC_URL plus that key; do not add the bucket name or prefix a second time to the base URL.

If using a new custom hostname, have the developer add it to images.remotePatterns in next.config.ts before building. The current list allows *.r2.dev, cdn.sutracore.space, and the QR-image provider. Uploads go browser → app /api/upload → R2; this flow does not need browser-to-R2 upload CORS configuration.

Verify with a small image upload in Profile, save the profile, and confirm the returned image URL opens in a browser. A successful write with a broken image usually points to the public URL, public-access settings, object path, or image-host allowlist.

5. Resend email: domain and sender

This application uses Resend's API, not SMTP. Adding SMTP_HOST, SMTP_USER, or SMTP_PASSWORD will not configure its email sender.

In the customer's Resend Domains, add a sending domain/subdomain. Publish the DNS records Resend supplies at the domain's DNS provider, then wait for verification. Use the exact requested records and avoid replacing unrelated mail records. See Verified domains.

Create a dedicated sending API key in Resend API Keys and store it as RESEND_API_KEY. Use a verified-domain sender such as Svara AI <no-reply@mail.customer.example> for RESEND_FROM_EMAIL. Keep the API key private; see Resend API key management.

dotenv
RESEND_API_KEY=re_replace_with_customer_sending_key
RESEND_FROM_EMAIL="Svara AI <no-reply@mail.customer.example>"

The sender address is a From identity; setting it does not create an inbox. Email links use BETTER_AUTH_URL, so production emails must not point to localhost. The currently connected sender functions deliver OTP and workspace invitation emails. Other files under emails/ are templates and should not be assumed to send automatically.

Verify email delivery with an agreed test recipient: request a verification/reset OTP and invite a teammate, then inspect Resend logs. bun run email:dev opens a local template preview on port 3001; previewing a template does not prove successful delivery.

6. Stripe and unused historical variables

The runtime uses STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET, STRIPE_PRICE_PRO_MONTHLY_ID, and optional STRIPE_PRICE_ENTERPRISE_MONTHLY_ID. See document 05 for where to obtain each.

Historical .env files may also contain STRIPE_PRICE_FREE_MONTHLY_ID, STRIPE_PRODUCT_FREE_ID, STRIPE_PRODUCT_PRO_ID, and STRIPE_PRODUCT_ENTERPRISE_ID. These are not read by the current app runtime; they are outputs of the optional Stripe setup helper. Migration-only variables such as OLD_R2_*, OLD_CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID, NEW_DATABASE_URL, and POSTGRES_CONTAINER belong to the migration helper, not routine app startup.

Use one definition per variable. Remove duplicate assignments when preparing the customer's configuration, especially duplicate app URLs and Stripe price IDs.

7. Apply environment changes

Stop and restart the local Next.js process after editing .env. In production, update the hosting environment and redeploy/restart. Set NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables before the build; changing a runtime value alone may leave the old origin embedded in the client bundle. Keep all URL origins consistent and omit trailing slashes.

Implementation references: lib/db.ts, drizzle.config.ts, docker-compose.yml, lib/auth.ts, lib/auth-client.ts, lib/s3.ts, lib/resend.ts, lib/seo.ts, and next.config.ts.

Code examples and source locations

Where runtime credentials are read

ts
// lib/db.ts — database connection source.
const databaseUrl = process.env.DATABASE_URL;

// lib/resend.ts — server-only email configuration.
const resendApiKey = process.env.RESEND_API_KEY;
const resendFromEmail = process.env.RESEND_FROM_EMAIL;
const resend = resendApiKey ? new Resend(resendApiKey) : null;

// lib/s3.ts — public image path settings, separate from secret access keys.
export const R2_BUCKET = process.env.R2_BUCKET ?? "";
export const R2_PUBLIC_URL = process.env.R2_PUBLIC_URL ?? "";

These are excerpts from separate files. Preserve their existing imports and validation. Local values come from the root .env; the host supplies corresponding environment variables in production. There is no settings-panel form that writes these credentials.

Allow a new customer image hostname

After connecting the customer's R2 public domain, add its hostname to the existing images.remotePatterns array in next.config.ts. This is a customization example; keep the other required entries:

ts
{
  protocol: "https",
  hostname: "assets.customer.example",
},

Set R2_PUBLIC_URL=https://assets.customer.example separately in the environment. The allowlist entry takes only the hostname, while the environment value includes the protocol. Rebuild/redeploy after changing the Next.js configuration.

Customize email subjects

lib/resend.ts contains the existing OTP subject map. Edit the human-readable values, keeping the type keys unchanged:

ts
const emailSubjectByType: Record<OtpEmailType, string> = {
  "sign-in": "Your sign-in OTP code",
  "email-verification": "Verify your email address",
  "forget-password": "Reset your password with OTP",
  "change-email": "Confirm your email change",
};

Email sender identity is RESEND_FROM_EMAIL; email layout, logo, wording, and inline colors are customized in emails/. See Branding and app configuration.

07 — Installation, copying the app, and ZIP release

Code examples and source files ↓

Documentation index · Previous: Environment and services · Next: Launch checks

1. Understand the deliverables

The customer receives source code and this illustrated guide. Existing database records, stored uploads, service credentials, and Stripe account ownership must be handled separately.

After setup, a verified, onboarded customer should reach a dashboard with this structure. The numbers shown are sample data, not a database-restore check.

2. Create a source ZIP on the current computer

Open PowerShell in the application folder and run the included packaging helper:

powershell
Set-Location 'C:\Workspace\JS\svara-app'
.\docs\scripts\create-release.ps1

The script prints the ZIP's full path and SHA-256 checksum. Its default output is beside the application folder, with a timestamp in the filename. It packages the current files, including current uncommitted source edits. It does not modify Git, the source, or service configuration. Review the source changes you intend to deliver before packaging.

To choose the destination explicitly:

powershell
.\docs\scripts\create-release.ps1 -OutputPath 'C:\CustomerDelivery\svara-app-final-release.zip'

Create the destination folder first. The helper refuses to overwrite an existing archive and verifies the resulting entry names against its exclusion rules. It includes an outer svara-app folder for straightforward extraction.

Include Exclude
app, components, emails, hooks, lib, public node_modules, .next, build/output/cache folders
scripts, drizzle, docs, package.json, bun.lock .git, editor/local hosting state, unrelated reference folders
Root configuration and .gitignore; the product README is in docs/ Real .env/.env.* files, keys/certificates, dumps, logs, archives
docs/config/.env.example with placeholders only Database volume contents and service-account secrets

The script uses an explicit list of source folders and root files. If future development adds another required root folder/file, update that list before packaging. It checks filenames, not the meaning of source text; a developer must still ensure no secrets are hardcoded in deliverable source.

If PowerShell blocks local script execution under the customer's policy, follow their administrator-approved script process or use the manual approach below; no permanent policy change is needed by this guide.

3. Manual ZIP and folder-copy approach

  1. Create a separate staging folder, for example C:\CustomerDelivery\svara-app.
  2. Copy the Include items listed above from the original folder into staging. Do not copy the original .env, dependencies, generated builds, dumps, or local caches.
  3. Keep docs/screenshots beside the Markdown documents; otherwise their images will not open. The HTML reader embeds its own screenshots.
  4. Review staging for secrets and confirm package.json, bun.lock, app source, configuration, and documentation are present.
  5. In Explorer, right-click the staging svara-app folder and select Compress to ZIP file (or the Windows version's Send to → Compressed (zipped) folder).
  6. Transfer the ZIP and checksum to the intended customer through the agreed delivery channel. Transfer credentials through the customer's secret-management channel separately.

For a direct folder copy instead of ZIP, use the same staging contents. Do not copy a live node_modules directory between computers; reinstall from the lockfile on the destination.

4. Extract and install prerequisites

The customer needs a Node.js version compatible with Next.js 16 (20.9 or newer), Bun for the checked-in lockfile, and access to PostgreSQL. Use the delivery team's tested runtime versions; this repository does not pin them. Docker Desktop/Engine is needed only for the bundled local database approach.

Extract the ZIP, open the extracted svara-app folder in a terminal, and check/install dependencies:

powershell
node --version
bun --version
bun install --frozen-lockfile

The repository supplies bun.lock, so Bun is the reproducible install path. npm install is an alternative, but it resolves without an npm lockfile and creates a new package-lock.json; have the developer validate that dependency set before using it for release.

See Next.js installation requirements.

5. Create configuration

Copy docs/config/.env.example to the root .env and fill in the values using document 06. Configure Resend before registering a fresh account, because email verification is required. Configure R2 before uploading images. Stripe is optional for initial Free-account access, but needed for paid billing.

For production, choose the final HTTPS origin, set the public URL variables before building, and add the customer image hostname to next.config.ts when required.

6. Initialize a NEW local database

These steps apply to a new empty development/customer database, not an existing production database.

powershell
docker compose up -d postgres
docker compose ps
bun run db:push

Wait until PostgreSQL is healthy before running db:push. Review the proposed schema operations. The source of truth is lib/db/schema.ts, as selected by drizzle.config.ts; auth-schema.ts is not the configured Drizzle schema.

db:push creates the schema but does not insert the default plan rows. Seed them before the first onboarding/workspace creation:

powershell
Get-Content -Raw '.\docs\scripts\initialize-plans.sql' | docker compose exec -T postgres sh -c 'psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1'

For a new managed PostgreSQL database, use the same DATABASE_URL for db:push and run initialize-plans.sql through the provider's SQL console or a trusted PostgreSQL client. The supplied SQL inserts missing default plan definitions only; it does not replace existing custom limits.

Do not blindly execute every historical SQL migration in filename order: this repository contains both 0004_plan_allowance.sql and 0005_cuddly_jasper_sitwell.sql with overlapping table creation. For upgrades to an existing database, take a backup and have the developer prepare a reviewed migration path. This release does not execute schema changes on the current database.

7. Start and confirm access

For development:

powershell
bun run dev

Open http://localhost:3000/auth/signin. On a fresh database, use Sign up, verify the email, sign in, and complete onboarding. There is no automatic seed for the demo account. If onboarding reaches the known missing /billing/plan route, open /dashboard and have the developer correct the redirect.

For a production Node.js deployment:

powershell
bun run build
bun run start

Run the production process under the hosting provider's service/process management with HTTPS, persistent database access, configured environment variables, and the public Stripe webhook. The Compose file does not deploy Next.js, configure a reverse proxy, provide certificates, or configure backups. Hosting the app on Cloudflare itself needs a deployment adapter/platform decision; the current Cloudflare integration is R2 storage only.

8. Move existing data and files separately

If transferring existing customer data, arrange a PostgreSQL backup/restore and R2 object migration in addition to the source ZIP. Preserve object paths or update stored image URLs when the bucket/domain/prefix changes. Stripe customers/subscriptions stay in their Stripe account and require a separate continuity plan if that account changes.

The existing scripts/migrate_to_new_instance.py supports R2 copy, database transfer, and URL rewriting. It requires boto3, python-dotenv, source Docker PostgreSQL, old R2 values, target R2 values, and NEW_DATABASE_URL. Review its source and begin with its documented dry run:

powershell
python scripts/migrate_to_new_instance.py all --dry-run

Do not use its --force option as routine setup; it can drop target database tables. A source ZIP is not a database backup. Keep encrypted backups and test restoration independently.

9. Complete delivery

Record the ZIP checksum, deployed URL, runtime versions, service-account owners, database backup location, R2 bucket/domain, Stripe mode/webhook URL, support contact, and unresolved issues. Record secret-store references rather than secret values. Complete the checklist in document 08 with the customer.

Code examples and source locations

Application commands

These selected commands already exist under scripts in package.json. This is a reference excerpt, not a replacement for the whole scripts object:

json
{
  "dev": "next dev",
  "build": "next build",
  "start": "next start",
  "brand:generate": "node scripts/generate-brand-assets.mjs",
  "db:push": "drizzle-kit push"
}

Run bun run brand:generate only after editing the brand mark or generator colors as described in document 09. Schema push is for the reviewed new-database setup above; it is not a backup/restore operation.

Packaging scope

If a later feature adds a required source folder, update the explicit include list in docs/scripts/create-release.ps1:

powershell
# Existing list in create-release.ps1:
$folders = @('app', 'components', 'emails', 'hooks', 'lib', 'public', 'scripts', 'drizzle', 'docs')

Keep the credential/build-output exclusion rules in that script. Add required root files to $rootFiles separately. Before delivery, rebuild the reader and package the resulting docs alongside the source:

powershell
node .\docs\scripts\build-guide.cjs
node .\docs\scripts\verify-docs.cjs
.\docs\scripts\create-release.ps1

The helper prints an archive path and SHA-256. Verify an archive's checksum with:

powershell
# Replace this example path with the path printed by the helper.
Get-FileHash -LiteralPath 'C:\CustomerDelivery\svara-app-final-release.zip' -Algorithm SHA256

08 — Launch checks, current limitations, and support

Code examples and source files ↓

Documentation index · Previous: Installation and ZIP · Next: Branding and configuration

1. What was reviewed

The documentation review used the supplied local test login on 31 October 2026. It confirmed sign-in, dashboard navigation, all eight settings panels, workspace forms, the existing workspace selector, a subscribed workspace's Billing Overview, and an alternate workspace's plan selection page. Authentication forms were captured while signed out. The original workspace was restored before signing out.

No OTP or invitation email was sent. No account was created or deleted, no password/2FA/passkey was changed, no workspace content was saved, and no payment, subscription, deployment, or database migration was performed. First-time onboarding was inspected in source because the supplied account is already onboarded. Provider screenshots show public help pages only. This is a documentation release, not a production-readiness certification.

2. Acceptance checklist

The delivery team and customer should record a result for each applicable check:

  • Extract the source ZIP on the customer's machine and verify its checksum.
  • Confirm real .env values and private keys are absent from the source archive.
  • Confirm customer ownership/access for hosting, DNS, database, R2, Resend, and Stripe.
  • Install dependencies from bun.lock; record Node.js/Bun versions.
  • Configure database access and seed default plan definitions on a new database.
  • Complete a production build and start the intended hosting process.
  • Register a controlled customer test user, receive OTP, verify, sign in, and complete onboarding.
  • Correct onboarding return URLs and test the full Pro onboarding path.
  • Confirm all production links, canonical URLs, email links, and checkout returns use the customer domain.
  • Upload/save a small profile image and workspace logo, then load their public URLs.
  • Create/switch/edit a workspace with the intended owner role; verify permissions with a member account.
  • Send/accept an invitation with a controlled recipient and verify the correct active workspace.
  • Correct invitation expiry and duplicate-acceptance handling in the custom join endpoint.
  • Test OTP password recovery with a controlled account.
  • Replace external TOTP QR generation; then test 2FA setup, sign-in, and backup codes.
  • Register/test a passkey on the final production domain with a controlled account.
  • Complete sandbox billing tests, verify webhook delivery, reconcile subscription and allowance records, and test portal access.
  • Confirm agreed live Stripe prices/currency match the app's displayed prices before accepting payments.
  • Remove demo credentials/prefills and arrange the test-account retirement process.
  • Agree which placeholder/disabled features are outside the delivered customer scope.
  • Test database/R2 restoration and record support and renewal responsibilities.

3. Current source and data limitations

Finding Customer impact / required follow-up
Onboarding uses /billing/plan, but the implemented route is /billing/plans New-user and Pro-checkout return paths can end on a missing page; correct the source URLs
Demo credentials are displayed on public auth pages and prefilled in sign-in Remove the demo card and blank the public prefill variables before launch; handle the test account separately
Google/GitHub UI exists without server socialProviders Configure and test OAuth in code, or remove/disable those entry points
Dashboard metrics are hardcoded; three analytics tabs are placeholders They do not represent live customer analytics
Several sidebar items, report/search actions, and top-left Create workspace are unwired Use Setting → Workspace for creation; agree feature scope before release
Account password-update button is disabled Use the OTP password-reset flow
Two-factor setup sends a secret URI to an external QR service Generate QR codes locally before production use
Custom invitation acceptance lacks an explicit expiry comparison and does not explicitly switch the active organization Review expiry, repeat acceptance, and workspace-selection behavior
Billing authorization in lib/auth.ts accepts any workspace membership Do not promise owner-only billing controls; tighten role checks if that is the customer requirement
Existing demo Billing says Pro while allowance/sidebar says Free Reconcile records and webhook processing; legacy screenshot state is not proof of correct billing
Billing's Active badge also covers past_due records Check actual Stripe status/invoices rather than relying on this badge
Plan features advertise API keys, SSO, and advanced analytics Entitlement labels are not proof those customer-facing features exist
Historical SQL includes overlapping allowance-table creation Use a reviewed upgrade path; new setup uses schema push plus missing-plan seeding
Account/workspace deletion is separate from provider billing/storage Review ownership, cancel/manage subscriptions, and handle stored files explicitly

These findings were documented, not changed as part of this task.

4. Troubleshooting

Symptom Checks and recovery
DATABASE_URL is not configured Place .env beside package.json, check the variable spelling, then restart the app
Database connection refused Start PostgreSQL, wait for health, check host/port, database credentials, firewall, and required TLS settings
Missing table on a new installation Confirm DATABASE_URL points to the new database, then initialize the schema with the reviewed db:push step
Free plan_allowance row missing Run docs/scripts/initialize-plans.sql against the initialized new database before onboarding
Email not verified / no OTP Use Verify email → Resend OTP; inspect Resend domain, sender, key, logs, and spam folder
Password reset appears to do nothing Request OTP first, then follow Reset password and complete that form; the settings password button is disabled
Google/GitHub sign-in fails Server OAuth providers are not configured in this version
Redirects go to localhost after deployment Align app/auth/public URL variables, rebuild the client bundle, and restart/redeploy
Onboarding ends on a 404 Open /dashboard or /billing; correct the source's singular /billing/plan URLs
Image upload returns 401 Sign in again; uploads require a valid session
R2 upload fails Check account ID, bucket, S3 key pair, bucket-scoped write permission, and endpoint jurisdiction
Uploaded image does not display Check R2_PUBLIC_URL, object key/prefix, public access, and the Next.js image-host allowlist
Workspace name/slug/mobile/email already exists Use a unique value; the app enforces uniqueness
Invite does not join the workspace Use the invited email, reopen the original link after registration, inspect pending state, and select the workspace explicitly
Workspace/member limit reached Confirm the applicable plan and allowance; review limits in document 02
Invalid Stripe configuration Use a server sk_/rk_ key, whsec_ signing secret, and price_ Pro ID from the same account/environment
Paid checkout completes but sidebar remains Free Inspect webhook delivery/signature, workspace reference, subscription row, and organization allowance; do not solve by manually editing only a UI label
Billing portal unavailable Confirm the workspace has the expected Stripe customer/subscription and that portal configuration is saved in the matching environment
Passkey works locally but not on the customer domain Register it again on the final domain; verify HTTPS and device/browser support
Changes to .env are ignored Restart the server; rebuild/redeploy for NEXT_PUBLIC_* changes; check duplicate variable definitions
A ?tab=workspace link still shows Profile Click Workspace explicitly; the current settings component does not parse the tab query parameter

5. Information to collect for support

Give support the page URL/path, action taken, exact error text, timestamp with timezone, browser version, deployment/version identifier, and a redacted screenshot. For provider issues, include a non-secret event/request ID when available. Do not include passwords, OTPs, secret keys, session tokens, TOTP URIs, backup codes, a raw .env, or an unredacted database dump.

Read-only setup checks

Run these from the application root when collecting installation information. They show versions/status and whether configuration files exist; they do not print .env contents or revoke sessions:
